The first generic train was poor: only octane sold and six columns cost $440M/yr. Blend values are ~$185M C4, $648M C5, $1045M C6 paraffin, $396M naphthene at full recovery. Now testing sharper cuts (root/B 40 stages R3, difficult C6 split 60/R4) while dropping the unprofitable octane/nonane columns. C3 and C7+ may remain unsold initially.

note: Rebuild around the two most valuable blends with much sharper cuts, eliminating all unproductive polishing columns.

Five loose columns earned nothing and cost $534M/yr. C4-/C5 and C5/C6 cuts leaked badly at 40 stages/R3. Potential blend revenues are about $619M C5 and $1115M C6 paraffin, so these two cuts plus a root split should support a profitable core. Light products and heavy tail remain unsold for now.

note: Increase boil-up at the first two columns to move the cuts from within C4/C5 to the intended C5/C6 and C4/C5 boundaries while retaining the effective C6-paraffin split.

The initial root at 60/5/5 cut near C4/C5, not C5/C6, leaving 26% N-pentane in the C6 blend. The T column likewise cut within C4 rather than C4/C5. B itself made a nearly correct C6-paraffin cut, so no change there yet. If root and T cuts move as intended, C5 and C6-paraffin blend revenue is about $1.75B/yr against roughly $0.6B/yr cost.

note: Move the root cut above the C6 paraffins and the second-column cut below C4 by adjusting boil-up in opposite directions, while leaving the promising C6 split unchanged.
notebook:

The root at 80/5/10 put 164 mol/s DMB in T and B was only 1476 versus the ideal 1739 C6+ flow. T at 60/4/8 sent 1066 mol/s overhead versus ideal 864 C4-. Root needs stronger boil-up; T needs less. Next add a C3/C4 split only if the corrected light stream is clean enough.

note: Correct the root cut while shrinking the easy C5/C6 and C4/C5 columns, and concentrate separation effort on the difficult C6-paraffin/naphthene boundary.
